new_statements.quote: [p.128] ...there are large numbers of Ila speaking peoples, in addition, including the Basala, Bambala, Balumbu, etc. [p.144] § 28. The question of stress in Ila presents considerable difficulty. As has been observed in the previous paragraph, in emphasis and repetition for clearness, the phenomenon of two adjacent stressed syllables in one word has been noticed. Apart from this, however, the main stress in Ila normally falls on the penultimate syllable. When this is the case I have left the stress unmarked ; but there are numerous cases of ultimate main stress, e.g. iji (egg) maji (eggs) vóse (all of them)

new_statements.rule_in_words: PROXY ONLY (Ila, ilaa1246): main word stress normally on the penultimate syllable, with a fair number of lexical items showing final main stress; one main stress per word. No statement specific to Sala exists in any source located; Doke and Smith & Dale subsume the Basala under 'Ila-speaking peoples', and Kashoki & Mann 1978 (p.70) say generically that Zambian Bantu syllables are near-evenly stressed with at most slight penultimate prominence tied to penultimate lengthening, never distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Doke p.143-144: emphatic/phrase-final lengthening of the final syllable (noted especially at Mala) may carry a secondary stress so that penult and ultima are both stressed, but 'there is still but one main stress on the word'. Smith & Dale 1920: 281 add a secondary stress on the stem vowel in long words.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Numerous cases of ultimate main stress' (iji 'egg', maji 'eggs', vose 'all of them'); raised tone on the first syllable of trisyllables (mahuta 'fat') and raised/level final tone (manga 'twins') give a false impression of stress; some speakers (Mala) show final as well as penultimate stress. Smith & Dale: monosyllabic enclitics draw stress to the final syllable (amb'ila vs uambila'nzhi), and stress can distinguish 'aze 'with him' from a'ze 'he also'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms of Ila proper (informants from Namwala, Kasenga, Mala, 1927); interacts with phrase-final emphatic lengthening. Applies to Sala only by the authors' ethnographic claim that the Basala speak Ila; Sala (Ila-Sala 93% shared basic vocabulary per Lehmann in Kashoki 1978) has no description of its own.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Sala (sala1266) itself. The quoted stress statement is for Ila proper (ilaa1246; Doke's 1927 informants from Namwala, Kasenga and Mala), extended to the Basala only by Doke's (1928: 128) and Smith's (1907) remark that the Basala are among the 'Ila-speaking peoples'. Glottolog/Ethnologue/Maho 2009 treat Sala as a separate language of the Ila-Lundwe-Sala cluster (M631); Lehmann in Kashoki 1978 reports 93% shared basic vocabulary Ila-Sala. The Kashoki & Mann 1978 statement is generic for all Zambian Bantu languages.
